To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose a novel IL algorithm, Primal Wasserstein Immitation Learning (PWI), that matches the behavior of an expert in a sample efficient and robust way.

we propose a new imitation learning algorithm, Primal Wasserstein imitation learning (PWIL), based on the primal Wasserstein distance, and that PWIL can match expert behavior with the Wasserstein metric, as opposed to the commonly used performance metric.

(i) the Wasserstein distance can be used to learn a reward function for imitation learning; (ii) the Wasserstein reward function is sample efficient; and (iii) the agent trained on the Wasserstein reward learns to imitate the expert behavior with the Wasserstein metric, rather than the performance metric.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel algorithm for imitation learning which has a simple formulation and is sample efficient, while being able to match expert behavior with the Wasserstein metric, rather than with performance.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we propose an algorithm that is simple, sample efficient, and that is able to match expert behavior in a principled way, and that we show that it works on a variety of challenging tasks.
PWIL is an algorithm that learns a reward function that matches that of the expert, and that the agent behavior matches that of the agent in terms of the Wasserstein metric.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we propose a novel IL method which is sample-efficient in terms of agent and expert interactions, which requires little fine tuning of the hyperparameters, which is robust to noise and which matches the behavior of an expert with the Wassersten distance, rather than with the commonly used proxy metric of performance.
we propose an imitation learning algorithm that can learn from an expert that has been trained using a policy gradient method.
we propose a new algorithm for imitation learning that matches expert behavior in a sample efficient way and with the Wasserstein loss, rather than with a performance proxy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we show that a conceptually simple method can be used for IL in a variety of continuous tasks, while achieving a sample efficient behavior matching.
we provide a simple, effective, and theoretically grounded algorithm for imitation learning in continuous control domains.
we can learn a policy which is close to an expert in a distribution sense and not only in a sample mean sense, which is the case for many IL algorithms.
